title: QuestDB 10.1: less I/O for late data, and more analysis in SQL
summary: QuestDB 10.1 adds merge-append partitions, which cut disk I/O and make late data readable sooner, brings SUBSAMPLE and exact percentiles to SQL, keeps a history of its own metrics, and runs GROUP BY over joins in parallel.
body_markdown:
QuestDB is the open-source time-series database for demanding workloads—from trading floors to mission control. It delivers ultra-low latency, high ingestion throughput, and a multi-tier storage engine. Native support for Parquet and SQL keeps your data portable, AI-ready—no vendor lock-in.


---


QuestDB is happiest when data arrives in order. Live data, on the other hand, often arrives out of order, especially when it comes from several feeds or from parallel senders. When that happens, QuestDB has to write the affected partitions again with the late rows merged in. Meanwhile a lot of everyday analysis still happens just outside the database: a chart library thinning millions of points, a notebook computing a p99 that SQL could only approximate, a separate monitoring stack collecting QuestDB's own metrics.


QuestDB 10.1 writes late data with less I/O and makes it readable sooner, and brings those other jobs into SQL.


Warning


10.1 has more breaking changes than a usual point release. Most turn a query that quietly returned the wrong thing into an error, but a few change results. Readthe list before upgrading, especially if you use` HORIZON JOIN` , INT arithmetic or interval strings like` '1min'` .


---


## QuestDB 10.1 at a glance


**Merge-append partitions :** A late write into an older partition no longer has to write that partition out again. QuestDB appends the rows it touches and folds the partition back together in the background, trading some temporary disk space for much less disk I/O, and since each write has less to do, new rows are readable sooner. It's opt-in, with one configuration setting.


**SUBSAMPLE :** A new SQL clause that picks the most significant rows of a result and returns them unchanged. For a chart, that's the few hundred rows that keep its shape out of millions. It also works for error-bounded compression and archiving.


**Exact percentiles :**` percentile_disc()` and` percentile_cont()` , as aggregates and window functions, with several percentile levels in one pass. Unlike` approx_percentile()` , they accept negative values.


**Metrics history in sys.metrics :** QuestDB writes its own metrics to a table every second. Put a notebook on top and you have monitoring with no metrics aggregator and no dashboard server.


**HORIZON JOIN changes :** Markout queries return one row per trade and offset, and can filter the quotes they match against, such as a single venue's. Both changes might alter the results of existing queries, so if you use` HORIZON JOIN` , it's worth reading that section before you upgrade.


**Parallel GROUP BY over joins :** Aggregating over a join now uses every query worker, with no change to the query.


**Lists in variables :** A` DECLARE` variable can hold a list for` IN` , which makes notebook dashboards filterable by a set of symbols.


**And more :** Faster` LATEST ON` , faster pattern filters on indexed symbols,` lag()` over symbols, and a long list of correctness fixes.


That's 10.1 in brief. If it's all you need, read thebreaking changes and go straight togetting 10.1 . Otherwise, the sections below cover each change in more detail, with queries you can run on the demo.


---


## Merge-append partitions: late data without the rewrite


Late data is normal in time-series work. Several writers feed the same table and their batches overlap in time, a venue reconnects and replays forty minutes from earlier in the day, a device comes back online with an hour of buffered readings, or a backfill fills a gap from last week. QuestDB keeps each partition sorted by time, so a commit with rows for a partition that's already on disk has always meant writing a new copy of that partition with the late rows merged in. A few thousand late rows can cost a rewrite of millions, and a steady trickle of them keeps the disk busy rewriting the same partitions.


With` cairo.o3.partition.merge.append.enabled=true` , the late commit instead takes the slice of the partition its rows fall into, merges the late rows into that slice, and appends the result to the end of the partition's column files. The partition then points at the new copy of that slice. A partition can hold several of these **pieces** over one set of files, much like Parquet row groups, and the rows they replaced stay behind as dead space until a background compaction folds the partition back into one piece.


The public demo has run with merge-append since 22 October. Before that, it wrote about 440 rows to disk for every row it ingested, most of it from refreshing materialized views. Since the switch, it writes about 8:


Rows written to disk per row ingested on the demo, in 15-minute buckets. Each day the ratio climbed to around 1,000, a daily average of about 440, until merge-append was switched on during 22 October. Since then it has stayed at about 8.


Less rewriting pays off twice. The disk does less work, and because each WAL apply has less to write, rows become readable sooner after they're ingested. On the demo, the median time to apply a batch fell from 1.7 ms to 0.6 ms, and the average from 5.5 ms to 3.0 ms.


The chart comes fromsys.metrics , also new in 10.1, so you can watch the same ratio on your own instance before and after turning merge-append on. Its counters are cumulative, so the query takes the difference between consecutive rows:


Rows written to disk per row ingested, from sys.metrics


[Demo this query](https://demo.questdb.io/?query=WITH%20d%20AS%20(%0A%20%20SELECT%20ts%2C%0A%20%20%20%20wal_apply_physically_written_rows%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20-%20lag(wal_apply_physically_written_rows)%20OVER%20(ORDER%20BY%20ts)%20AS%20written%2C%0A%20%20%20%20wal_apply_written_rows%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20-%20lag(wal_apply_written_rows)%20OVER%20(ORDER%20BY%20ts)%20AS%20ingested%0A%20%20FROM%20%27sys.metrics%27%0A%20%20WHERE%20ts%20IN%20%27%24now%20-%207d..%24now%27%0A)%0ASELECT%20ts%2C%20sum(written)%20%2F%20sum(ingested)%20AS%20amplification%0AFROM%20d%0AWHERE%20written%20%3E%3D%200%20AND%20ingested%20%3E%200%0ASAMPLE%20BY%2015m%3B%0A&executeQuery=true)


```text
WITH d AS (     SELECT ts,       wal_apply_physically_written_rows         - lag(wal_apply_physically_written_rows) OVER (ORDER BY ts) AS written,       wal_apply_written_rows         - lag(wal_apply_written_rows) OVER (ORDER BY ts) AS ingested     FROM 'sys.metrics'     WHERE ts IN '$now - 7d..$now'   )   SELECT ts, sum(written) / sum(ingested) AS amplification   FROM d   WHERE written >= 0 AND ingested > 0   SAMPLE BY 15m;
```


` deadRows` ,` pieceCount` and` lastWriteTimestamp` are new columns in[table_partitions()](https://questdb.com/docs/query/functions/meta/#table_partitions) and` SHOW PARTITIONS` , so you can see where dead space is building up:


Partitions with pieces and dead rows


[Demo this query](https://demo.questdb.io/?query=SELECT%20name%2C%20numRows%2C%20deadRows%2C%20pieceCount%2C%20lastWriteTimestamp%0AFROM%20table_partitions(%27fx_trades%27)%0AWHERE%20pieceCount%20%3E%201%3B%0A&executeQuery=true)


```text
SELECT name, numRows, deadRows, pieceCount, lastWriteTimestamp   FROM table_partitions('fx_trades')   WHERE pieceCount > 1;
```


On an hourly-partitioned table like this one, the only partition that shows pieces, if any, is the hour being written, with a handful of dead rows from slightly late rows in the feed. The earlier hours are back to a single piece.


The folding is done by a new` partition-compaction` worker, which checks WAL tables every two minutes. It builds the compacted copy from a reader snapshot and swaps it in as a metadata change, so ingestion doesn't pause. It runs whether or not merge-append is on, because it also cleans up idle Parquet partitions with dead row groups, and merges partitions that out-of-order writes split in the middle once they go idle.


Three things to know before turning it on:


- **It trades disk space for write amplification.** Between a late write and the next compaction, a partition takes more space than its live rows.
- **It's off by default.** The[merge-append docs](https://questdb.com/docs/concepts/merge-append-partitions/) cover when it helps and how to enable it. We'd like to hear how it behaves on your late data.
- **Rolling back takes some preparation.** QuestDB versions before 10.1 refuse a table that still has merge-append partitions. The[downgrade steps](https://questdb.com/docs/concepts/merge-append-partitions/#downgrade-safely) explain what to do first.


---


## SUBSAMPLE: keep the rows that matter


[SUBSAMPLE](https://questdb.com/docs/query/sql/subsample/) picks the most significant rows of a query result and drops the rest.` SAMPLE BY` aggregates each time bucket, so what you get is a` min()` ,` max()` or` avg()` per bucket rather than values from real rows.` SUBSAMPLE` selects real rows from the data, each with its original timestamp and all its columns.


What "most significant" means depends on the method. For a line chart, it means the rows that best preserve the shape of the line: the peaks, the troughs and the turns, and not the points in the middle of a smooth run. Here's one day of EURUSD trades on the demo, 682,348 of them, compressed with` sdt` at four tolerances, each in a cell of the same Web Console notebook:


One day of EURUSD trades, 682,348 rows, reduced by SUBSAMPLE sdt to 4,532, 546, 243 and 65 rows. Each query ran in about 45 ms on the demo.


As the tolerance grows, the noise goes first and the larger moves stay.` sdt` , Swinging Door Trending, comes from the process historians used in industrial plants. Instead of a row count it takes a tolerance in the units of the column, and keeps as few rows as it can while guaranteeing that a straight line between the kept rows never strays further than twice that tolerance from any row it dropped.


That guarantee is what makes` SUBSAMPLE` useful beyond charts. A tolerance of 0.0005 keeps 82,023 of those 682,348 trades, and any price in between can be reconstructed to within 0.001. Written to another table, that's a compressed archive with a known error:


Archive yesterday's EURUSD prices to within 0.001


```text
INSERT INTO fx_trades_archive   SELECT timestamp, symbol, price   FROM fx_trades   WHERE symbol = 'EURUSD'     AND timestamp IN '$yesterday'   SUBSAMPLE sdt(price, 0.0005);
```


When the goal is a fixed number of points instead of a fixed error, the other methods take a target count:


Method Keeps


` lttb(col, n)` n rows that preserve the shape of a line


` m4(col, n)` up to n rows: first, last, min and max of each time slot


` minmax(col, n)` up to n rows: min and max of each time slot


` uniform(n)` n evenly spaced rows, including the first and last


` cadence(k)` every k-th row


` sdt(col, dev)` as few rows as the tolerance allows


` lttb` (Largest-Triangle-Three-Buckets) is the usual choice for a line chart, and` m4` keeps the exact visual envelope for a chart of a known pixel width.` SUBSAMPLE` runs after` SAMPLE BY` , so you can aggregate first and then thin the aggregate:


One-second average bids, thinned to 300 points


[Demo this query](https://demo.questdb.io/?query=SELECT%20timestamp%2C%20avg(best_bid)%20AS%20bid%0AFROM%20market_data%0AWHERE%20symbol%20%3D%20%27EURUSD%27%0A%20%20AND%20timestamp%20IN%20%27%24yesterday%27%0ASAMPLE%20BY%201s%0ASUBSAMPLE%20lttb(bid%2C%20300)%3B%0A&executeQuery=true)


```text
SELECT timestamp, avg(best_bid) AS bid   FROM market_data   WHERE symbol = 'EURUSD'     AND timestamp IN '$yesterday'   SAMPLE BY 1s   SUBSAMPLE lttb(bid, 300);
```


The[SUBSAMPLE reference](https://questdb.com/docs/query/sql/subsample/) has a diagram for each method and the full error guarantee for` sdt` .


---


## Exact percentiles: percentile_disc and percentile_cont


QuestDB has had` approx_percentile()` for a while. 10.1 adds the two SQL standard functions, closing one of our longest-open[feature requests](https://github.com/questdb/questdb/issues/1371) .[percentile_disc()](https://questdb.com/docs/query/functions/aggregation/#percentile_disc--quantile_disc) returns a value that's actually in the data, and[percentile_cont()](https://questdb.com/docs/query/functions/aggregation/#percentile_cont--quantile_cont) interpolates between the two nearest values. Here they are next to` approx_percentile()` at a low resolution:


Exact and approximate p99 price, and three trade size percentiles


[Demo this query](https://demo.questdb.io/?query=SELECT%20symbol%2C%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20percentile_cont(price%2C%200.99)%20AS%20p99_exact%2C%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20approx_percentile(price%2C%200.99%2C%201)%20AS%20p99_approx%2C%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20percentile_disc(quantity%2C%20ARRAY%5B0.5%2C%200.9%2C%200.99%5D)%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20AS%20size_p50_p90_p99%0AFROM%20fx_trades%0AWHERE%20timestamp%20IN%20%27%24yesterday%27%0A%20%20AND%20symbol%20IN%20(%27EURUSD%27%2C%20%27GBPUSD%27%2C%20%27USDJPY%27)%0AGROUP%20BY%20symbol%0AORDER%20BY%20symbol%3B%0A&executeQuery=true)


```text
SELECT symbol,          percentile_cont(price, 0.99) AS p99_exact,          approx_percentile(price, 0.99, 1) AS p99_approx,          percentile_disc(quantity, ARRAY[0.5, 0.9, 0.99])              AS size_p50_p90_p99   FROM fx_trades   WHERE timestamp IN '$yesterday'     AND symbol IN ('EURUSD', 'GBPUSD', 'USDJPY')   GROUP BY symbol   ORDER BY symbol;
```


symbol p99_exact p99_approx size_p50_p90_p99


EURUSD 1.1344 1.1250 \[111881.0, 238559.0, 504031.0\]


GBPUSD 1.3527 1.3125 \[112006.0, 239509.0, 505138.0\]


USDJPY 159.17 152.00 \[112552.0, 244294.0, 522504.0\]


The highlights:


- **Exact.** At precision 1,` approx_percentile()` puts the USDJPY p99 at 152.00 against an exact 159.17. Higher precision closes the gap, at the cost of more memory per group.
- **Negative values work.**` approx_percentile()` can't record a negative number, which rules it out for returns, spreads or P&L. The exact functions take any numeric input.
- **Several levels in one pass.** Pass an array and get every level back from one scan, like the trade sizes above. With` UNNEST` , ten deciles become a histogram in a single query.
- **Parallel.** Both run on every query worker in` GROUP BY` and` SAMPLE BY` .


Both also work as window functions over a whole partition, which puts each group's percentile next to every row:


Each trade against its pair's median price


[Demo this query](https://demo.questdb.io/?query=SELECT%20timestamp%2C%20symbol%2C%20price%2C%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20price%20-%20percentile_disc(price%2C%200.5)%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20OVER%20(PARTITION%20BY%20symbol)%20AS%20vs_median%0AFROM%20fx_trades%0AWHERE%20timestamp%20IN%20%27%24yesterday%27%0A%20%20AND%20symbol%20IN%20(%27EURUSD%27%2C%20%27USDJPY%27)%3B%0A&executeQuery=true)


```text
SELECT timestamp, symbol, price,          price - percentile_disc(price, 0.5)              OVER (PARTITION BY symbol) AS vs_median   FROM fx_trades   WHERE timestamp IN '$yesterday'     AND symbol IN ('EURUSD', 'USDJPY');
```


The window form doesn't take a rolling frame, and` approx_percentile()` has no window form.


With a` GROUP BY` , the exact functions run on every query worker, and they're usually faster than` approx_percentile()` , with the gap growing as the number of groups grows. Without a` GROUP BY` ,` approx_percentile()` is still faster on integer columns. It also uses less memory: the exact functions keep 8 bytes for every row, while the approximation keeps one fixed-size histogram per group. Our advice is to start with the exact functions, and switch to` approx_percentile()` when memory is tight or it's faster on your data, as long as its precision is enough and there are no negative values.` approx_percentile()` also gained the array form, and it now returns NULL for an empty group instead of another group's value.` quantile_disc()` and` quantile_cont()` work as aliases.


---


## sys.metrics: monitoring QuestDB from QuestDB


QuestDB now writes its global metrics to a` sys.metrics` table every second: about 160 counters and gauges covering queries, connections, ingestion, WAL apply, memory by allocation type, CPU and garbage collection. The table is partitioned by day with a one-week TTL, and it's written even when the Prometheus endpoint is off.


You query it like any other table. For example, peak CPU, memory and WAL apply rate per hour over the last twelve hours:


Peak CPU, memory and WAL apply rate per hour


[Demo this query](https://demo.questdb.io/?query=SELECT%20ts%2C%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20max(cpu_questdb_percent)%20AS%20peak_cpu_pct%2C%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20max(memory_rss)%20%2F%201073741824.0%20AS%20peak_rss_gib%2C%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20max(wal_apply_rows_per_second)%20AS%20peak_wal_rows_s%0AFROM%20%27sys.metrics%27%0AWHERE%20ts%20IN%20%27%24now%20-%2012h..%24now%27%0ASAMPLE%20BY%201h%3B%0A&executeQuery=true)


```text
SELECT ts,          max(cpu_questdb_percent) AS peak_cpu_pct,          max(memory_rss) / 1073741824.0 AS peak_rss_gib,          max(wal_apply_rows_per_second) AS peak_wal_rows_s   FROM 'sys.metrics'   WHERE ts IN '$now - 12h..$now'   SAMPLE BY 1h;
```


Put queries like that in a[Web Console notebook](https://questdb.com/docs/getting-started/web-console/notebooks/overview/) , draw them as charts and turn on auto-refresh, and you have a monitoring dashboard that lives in QuestDB itself, with no metrics aggregator and no dashboard server to run next to it. It's the same machinery as any other[live notebook dashboard](https://questdb.com/docs/getting-started/web-console/notebooks/live-dashboards/) . Here's one on the demo instance, refreshing every 30 seconds:


A monitoring dashboard on the demo, built from four sys.metrics queries in a Web Console notebook: WAL throughput, WAL backlog, CPU and open connections over the last 24 hours.


The table doesn't show up in` tables()` , so query it by name. The interval, the TTL, an exclude pattern and Parquet storage are set under` metrics.persist.*` ; see[persisted metrics](https://questdb.com/docs/operations/logging-metrics/#persisted-metrics) . It's the history of one instance, so for a fleet you still want Prometheus or a[Telegraf pipeline](https://questdb.com/docs/cookbook/operations/store-questdb-metrics/) that collects every instance in one place.


---


## HORIZON JOIN: one row per trade, and filters on the quotes


[HORIZON JOIN](https://questdb.com/docs/query/sql/horizon-join/) matches each trade with the prevailing quote at a list of offsets before and after it, which is what a markout curve is built from. The[time-series joins guide](https://questdb.com/blog/questdb-time-series-joins-guide/#horizon-join-what-happened-at-fixed-offsets-before-and-after-each-trade) covers it from scratch. Both changes in 10.1 might alter the results of existing queries.


**One row per trade and offset.** Without aggregate functions, it now returns[one row per left-hand row and offset](https://questdb.com/docs/query/sql/horizon-join/#queries-without-aggregate-functions) , duplicates included. Before, it grouped by the selected columns as if the query said` SELECT DISTINCT` , so two trades at the same price and time came back as one row.


Each EURUSD trade with the book at t, t+1s, t+5s and t+30s


[Demo this query](https://demo.questdb.io/?query=SELECT%20t.timestamp%2C%20t.symbol%2C%20t.side%2C%20t.price%2C%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20h.offset%20%2F%201_000_000_000%20AS%20horizon_s%2C%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20m.best_bid%2C%20m.best_ask%0AFROM%20fx_trades%20t%0AHORIZON%20JOIN%20market_data%20m%20ON%20(symbol)%0ALIST%20(0%2C%201s%2C%205s%2C%2030s)%20AS%20h%0AWHERE%20t.timestamp%20IN%20%27%24yesterday%27%0A%20%20AND%20t.symbol%20%3D%20%27EURUSD%27%3B%0A&executeQuery=true)


```text
SELECT t.timestamp, t.symbol, t.side, t.price,          h.offset / 1_000_000_000 AS horizon_s,          m.best_bid, m.best_ask   FROM fx_trades t   HORIZON JOIN market_data m ON (symbol)   LIST (0, 1s, 5s, 30s) AS h   WHERE t.timestamp IN '$yesterday'     AND t.symbol = 'EURUSD';
```


That's 682,348 trades and 2,729,392 rows, four per trade. The result keeps the trades' designated timestamp and order, so an outer query can run` SAMPLE BY` , another join or a window function over it. If you relied on the old shape, add` SELECT DISTINCT` or a` GROUP BY` , and run` REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW ... FULL` on any materialized view built on such a query. The docs have[upgrade steps](https://questdb.com/docs/query/sql/horizon-join/#upgrading-to-questdb-1010) .


**Filters on the quotes.** A predicate on the right-hand table in` ON` used to be **silently ignored** :` AND c.ecn = 'LMAX'` parsed fine, and the join matched against every venue anyway. Now it[filters the quotes before matching](https://questdb.com/docs/query/sql/horizon-join/#filtering-right-hand-tables) , so each trade gets the latest quote that passes the filter. Two venues can sit side by side in one query:


EURUSD markout in pips against LMAX and EBS quotes


[Demo this query](https://demo.questdb.io/?query=SELECT%20h.offset%20%2F%201_000_000_000%20AS%20horizon_s%2C%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20avg(CASE%20WHEN%20t.side%20%3D%20%27buy%27%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20THEN%20(l.bid_price%20%2B%20l.ask_price)%20%2F%202%20-%20t.price%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20ELSE%20t.price%20-%20(l.bid_price%20%2B%20l.ask_price)%20%2F%202%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20END)%20*%2010_000%20AS%20lmax_pips%2C%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20avg(CASE%20WHEN%20t.side%20%3D%20%27buy%27%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20THEN%20(e.bid_price%20%2B%20e.ask_price)%20%2F%202%20-%20t.price%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20ELSE%20t.price%20-%20(e.bid_price%20%2B%20e.ask_price)%20%2F%202%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20END)%20*%2010_000%20AS%20ebs_pips%0AFROM%20fx_trades%20t%0AHORIZON%20JOIN%20core_price%20l%0A%20%20%20%20ON%20(t.symbol%20%3D%20l.symbol%20AND%20l.ecn%20%3D%20%27LMAX%27)%0AHORIZON%20JOIN%20core_price%20e%0A%20%20%20%20ON%20(t.symbol%20%3D%20e.symbol%20AND%20e.ecn%20%3D%20%27EBS%27)%0ALIST%20(0%2C%201s%2C%205s%2C%2030s%2C%2060s)%20AS%20h%0AWHERE%20t.timestamp%20IN%20%27%24yesterday%27%0A%20%20AND%20t.symbol%20%3D%20%27EURUSD%27%0AORDER%20BY%20horizon_s%3B%0A&executeQuery=true)


```text
SELECT h.offset / 1_000_000_000 AS horizon_s,          avg(CASE WHEN t.side = 'buy'                   THEN (l.bid_price + l.ask_price) / 2 - t.price                   ELSE t.price - (l.bid_price + l.ask_price) / 2              END) * 10_000 AS lmax_pips,          avg(CASE WHEN t.side = 'buy'                   THEN (e.bid_price + e.ask_price) / 2 - t.price                   ELSE t.price - (e.bid_price + e.ask_price) / 2              END) * 10_000 AS ebs_pips   FROM fx_trades t   HORIZON JOIN core_price l       ON (t.symbol = l.symbol AND l.ecn = 'LMAX')   HORIZON JOIN core_price e       ON (t.symbol = e.symbol AND e.ecn = 'EBS')   LIST (0, 1s, 5s, 30s, 60s) AS h   WHERE t.timestamp IN '$yesterday'     AND t.symbol = 'EURUSD'   ORDER BY horizon_s;
```


The demo's venues are simulated from the same price process, so the two columns agree closely. On real venue data, this is the query that shows which venue's quotes your fills compare badly against.


A filtered table also works on the right-hand side,` HORIZON JOIN (core_price WHERE ecn = 'LMAX') l ON (...)` . A predicate on the left-hand table in` ON` was ignored the same way, and now fails with` unsupported HORIZON join expression` . It belongs in` WHERE` .


---


## GROUP BY over a join, on every core


Filters and` GROUP BY` over a single table have used every query worker in QuestDB for a long time. A` GROUP BY` over a join didn't: the join ran on one thread and fed the aggregation from there, while the other workers waited.


In 10.1, a` GROUP BY` or` SAMPLE BY` over a join of two tables on matching keys, the` ON t.symbol = d.symbol` kind, runs on all the query workers. QuestDB builds a lookup table from one side of the join once, and every worker matches its own share of the other side's rows against it and aggregates as it goes. Nothing changes in the query. Here, each pair's trades from yesterday are checked against the day before's range:


How many of yesterday's trades broke the previous day's range?


[Demo this query](https://demo.questdb.io/?query=SELECT%20t.symbol%2C%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20count()%20AS%20trades%2C%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20sum(CASE%20WHEN%20t.price%20%3E%20d.high%20THEN%201%20ELSE%200%20END)%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20AS%20above_prev_high%2C%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20sum(CASE%20WHEN%20t.price%20%3C%20d.low%20THEN%201%20ELSE%200%20END)%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20AS%20below_prev_low%0AFROM%20fx_trades%20t%0AJOIN%20(%0A%20%20SELECT%20symbol%2C%20high%2C%20low%0A%20%20FROM%20fx_trades_ohlc_1d%0A%20%20WHERE%20timestamp%20IN%20%27%24yesterday%20-%201d%27%0A)%20d%20ON%20t.symbol%20%3D%20d.symbol%0AWHERE%20t.timestamp%20IN%20%27%24yesterday%27%0AGROUP%20BY%20t.symbol%0AORDER%20BY%20trades%20DESC%0ALIMIT%205%3B%0A&executeQuery=true)


```text
SELECT t.symbol,          count() AS trades,          sum(CASE WHEN t.price > d.high THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)              AS above_prev_high,          sum(CASE WHEN t.price < d.low THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)              AS below_prev_low   FROM fx_trades t   JOIN (     SELECT symbol, high, low     FROM fx_trades_ohlc_1d     WHERE timestamp IN '$yesterday - 1d'   ) d ON t.symbol = d.symbol   WHERE t.timestamp IN '$yesterday'   GROUP BY t.symbol   ORDER BY trades DESC   LIMIT 5;
```

` EXPLAIN` shows the plan as` Async Hash Join Group By` , here with the demo's 46 workers. In the PR's benchmark, a 4M-row Parquet` LEFT JOIN` with a 400,000-row other side on 8 workers went from about 101 ms to about 50 ms, and its peak memory from 308 MB to 165 MB.


It covers` INNER` and` LEFT` joins, some` RIGHT` joins, and the common aggregates:` count()` ,` sum()` ,` avg()` ,` min()` ,` max()` , variance, standard deviation, correlation and` weighted_avg()` , among others. Order-dependent aggregates such as` first()` and` last()` , and` count_distinct()` , keep the old plan. The[configuration reference](https://questdb.com/docs/configuration/cairo-engine/#parallel-group-by-over-hash-joins) has the full rules, and` cairo.sql.parallel.hash.join.groupby.enabled=false` turns it off.

## Lists in DECLARE, for notebooks and dashboards


A` DECLARE` variable can now hold a list, used on the right-hand side of` IN` :


Name a set of symbols once


[Demo this query](https://demo.questdb.io/?query=DECLARE%20%40majors%20%3A%3D%20(%27EURUSD%27%2C%20%27GBPUSD%27%2C%20%27USDJPY%27)%0ASELECT%20symbol%2C%20count()%20AS%20trades%2C%20sum(quantity)%20AS%20volume%0AFROM%20fx_trades%0AWHERE%20timestamp%20IN%20%27%24yesterday%27%0A%20%20AND%20symbol%20IN%20%40majors%0AGROUP%20BY%20symbol%0AORDER%20BY%20symbol%3B%0A&executeQuery=true)


```text
DECLARE @majors := ('EURUSD', 'GBPUSD', 'USDJPY')   SELECT symbol, count() AS trades, sum(quantity) AS volume   FROM fx_trades   WHERE timestamp IN '$yesterday'     AND symbol IN @majors   GROUP BY symbol   ORDER BY symbol;
```

This is most useful in notebooks.[Notebook variables](https://questdb.com/docs/getting-started/web-console/notebooks/variables/) are built on` DECLARE` , so a variable like` @symbols := ('EURUSD', 'GBPUSD')` can now feed every cell that filters with` symbol IN @symbols` . On the designated timestamp, a declared list becomes an interval scan, the same as a written-out one. See[value lists](https://questdb.com/docs/query/sql/declare/#value-lists) .

## Faster queries and other changes


These numbers come from the benchmarks in each PR.


- **` LATEST ON` .** Filtered and multi-symbol` LATEST ON` queries ran 2.9x to 7.1x faster.` symbol = 'A' OR symbol = 'B'` is now planned like` symbol IN ('A', 'B')` , and a key filter outside a` LATEST ON` subquery is pushed inside it, so QuestDB only looks for the keys you asked for.
- **Pattern filters on indexed symbols.**` LIKE` ,` ILIKE` and regex filters, and their negations, can use a symbol index when the pattern matches few values. Selective patterns ran 35x to 73x faster. Broad patterns still scan.
- **` SAMPLE BY` with a time zone.** Calendar-aligned day buckets in a time zone with daylight saving run up to about 65% faster.
- **Late writes on XFS.** Out-of-order commits no longer wait on a synchronous disk allocation per column. Time in` posix_fallocate` during WAL apply fell from 2,171 ms to 28 ms in the PR's test.
- **Large QWP results.** A 50-million-row read over QWP used to peak at 6.40 GiB of server memory. The same read now peaks at 462 MiB and finishes 30% faster.
- **Fewer stalls.** Unmapping files no longer holds a process-wide lock, which removes a source of ingestion and query stalls.


**` lag()` and` lead()` over symbols.** Both now accept` SYMBOL` columns, including with` IGNORE NULLS` , which is what you need to spot a change of venue, side or regime from one row to the next:


How often does each pair's flow switch venue between trades?


[Demo this query](https://demo.questdb.io/?query=SELECT%20symbol%2C%20count()%20AS%20venue_switches%0AFROM%20(%0A%20%20SELECT%20symbol%2C%20ecn%2C%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20lag(ecn)%20OVER%20(PARTITION%20BY%20symbol%20ORDER%20BY%20timestamp)%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20AS%20prev_ecn%0A%20%20FROM%20fx_trades%0A%20%20WHERE%20timestamp%20IN%20%27%24yesterday%27%0A)%0AWHERE%20ecn%20!%3D%20prev_ecn%0AGROUP%20BY%20symbol%0AORDER%20BY%20venue_switches%20DESC%0ALIMIT%205%3B%0A&executeQuery=true)


```text
SELECT symbol, count() AS venue_switches   FROM (     SELECT symbol, ecn,            lag(ecn) OVER (PARTITION BY symbol ORDER BY timestamp)                AS prev_ecn     FROM fx_trades     WHERE timestamp IN '$yesterday'   )   WHERE ecn != prev_ecn   GROUP BY symbol   ORDER BY venue_switches DESC   LIMIT 5;
```

Outside SQL, browsers can now connect to QWP directly over a WebSocket, either same-origin with the session cookie or cross-origin through an allowlist. The bundled Web Console adds support for live views, a panel that lists running queries with their memory use and lets you cancel them, an option to run the whole query text, and rule-based trends in the result grid.


One change makes some joins slower. Joins on` SYMBOL` keys now keep their symbol lookup caches off-heap, where they're freed when the query ends and counted against the per-query memory limit. That uses less memory, but some queries might run slower.

## Before you upgrade: breaking changes in 10.1


Most of this list is QuestDB refusing a query it used to misread. The first three items can change results, so check those first.


- **` HORIZON JOIN` without aggregates.** One row per left row and offset. Use` SELECT DISTINCT` or` GROUP BY` for the old result, and` REFRESH ... FULL` on materialized views built on it.
- **` HORIZON JOIN`` ON` predicates.** Right-hand predicates now filter, left-hand ones fail with an error. Both used to be ignored.
- **INT arithmetic.** Wraps at 32 bits everywhere, including under a cast:` (100000 * 30000)::long` is` -1294967296` . Widen an operand, as in` 100000L * 30000` , for 64-bit math.
- **Malformed intervals.**` SAMPLE BY 1min` fails with` Invalid unit: 1min` . It used to be read as one nanosecond, and` 100ms` as one second. Use one-letter units:` 1m` ,` 100T` ,` 1d` .
- **` dateadd()` and the designated timestamp.** A` dateadd()` projection keeps the designated timestamp only for fixed-duration units over the designated column. Month and year units lose it, and views built on them become invalid.
- **` ORDER BY` expressions.** No longer returned as a hidden extra column.
- **` subsample` .** Reserved word. Quote it as` "subsample"` .
- **Window functions over` SYMBOL` .**` first_value()` ,` last_value()` ,` min()` ,` max()` and` nth_value()` over a symbol now fail to compile, as does` lag()` with a non-null default.` lag()` itself now works over symbols, asshown above .
- **` SAMPLE BY ... FILL` edge cases.**` first(ts) AS ts ... FILL(0)` now errors.
- **Parquet and cold partitions.**` UPDATE` on WAL tables with Parquet partitions,` ADD INDEX` with cold partitions and` ALTER COLUMN TYPE` with read-only ones are rejected instead of suspending the table.
- **` CREATE TABLE AS SELECT` over` LATEST ON` .** A partitioned CTAS that picks several keys from a` LATEST ON` subquery, on a symbol with a covering index, no longer infers the designated timestamp. Add` TIMESTAMP(col)` .
- **` table_partitions()` ,` SHOW PARTITIONS` ,` materialized_views()` .** New columns, so code that reads them by position needs updating.
- **HTTP sessions.** A request with a rejected` Authorization` header gets 401 and ends the session, instead of falling back to the cookie.
- **Platforms.** Intel (x86-64) macOS is no longer supported. macOS builds are Apple Silicon only.


The[10.1.0 release notes on GitHub](https://github.com/questdb/questdb/releases/tag/10.1.0) have the full list with PR links.
